query: Which material can be used for Temperature-dependent plastic deformation behaviors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy (HEA) exhibits a temperature‐dependent plastic deformation behavior in which the deformation mechanism shifts from dislocation nucleation and phase reorientation at low temperatures to thermally activated dislocation multiplication and twinning at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-prepared CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC structure (e.g., fabricated by selective laser melting or equivalent processing)
generation.intervention: Apply mechanical deformation (e.g., tensile or compressive loading) while systematically varying the testing temperature from cryogenic (around 77 K) to high temperatures (up to ~800 °C)
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under controlled strain rates in temperature-controlled environments that span cryogenic, room, and elevated temperature regimes
generation.structural_mediator: Activation and evolution of dislocation networks, twin boundaries, and phase reorientation regions (e.g., subtle shifts in preferred crystallographic orientation) that vary with temperature
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, the high surface energy and lattice distortion favor nucleation and propagation of partial dislocations and phase reorientation (as observed in nanowire studies), leading to superplastic-like behavior. At higher temperatures, thermal activation promotes dislocation mobility and suppresses complete phase reorientation, yet sustains sufficient plastic flow through increased dislocation multiplication and twinning, thereby balancing work hardening with ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy will show a clear change in stress–strain response with temperature: higher yield strength coupled with enhanced work hardening and evidence of phase reorientation/twinning mechanisms at low temperatures, and reduced yield strength but maintained ductility with thermally activated dislocation processes at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: Room temperature mechanical behavior characterized by a conventional balance of strength and ductility in CoCrFeMnNi HEA
generation.boundary: If temperatures are extended beyond the studied range (e.g., far beyond 800 °C or well below cryogenic conditions), phase stability might be compromised or the expected deformation mechanisms may no longer dominate, possibly invalidating the observed trends
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative changes in deformation mechanisms with temperature are supported by existing studies, precise quantitative differences in yield strength, ductility, and the relative contributions of dislocation versus twinning mechanisms require further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA samples with a uniform single-phase FCC microstructure. Perform a series of mechanical tests (tensile and/or compressive) at selected temperatures (e.g., 77 K, room temperature, and 800 °C) while using in-situ characterization techniques (such as transmission electron microscopy and electron backscatter diffraction) to monitor dislocation activity, twinning, and any phase reorientation processes.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rate from stress–strain curves
Dislocation density and twin/interphase boundary characteristics via TEM/EBSD
Any evidence of crystallographic reorientation (e.g., changes in preferred orientation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental results show no significant variation in the deformation mechanisms (e.g., no observable shift from dislocation nucleation to thermally activated processes) or if the yield strength and ductility remain essentially unchanged across the temperature range, then the hypothesis that temperature governs a switch in the plastic deformation mechanism in CoCrFeMnNi HEA is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High strength and ductility, often mutually exclusive properties of a structural material, are also responsible for damage tolerance. At low temperatures, due to high surface energy, single element metallic nanowires such as Ag usually transform into a more preferred phase via nucleation and propagation of partial dislocation through the nanowire, enabling superplasticity. In high entropy alloy (HEA) CoNiCrFeMn nanowires, the motion of the partial dislocation is hindered by the friction due to difference in the lattice parameter of the constituent atoms which is responsible for the hardening and lowering the ductility. In this study, we have examined the temperature-dependent superplasticity of single component Ag and multicomponent CoNiCrFeMn HEA nanowires using molecular dynamics simulations. The results demonstrate that Ag nanowires exhibit apparent temperature-dependent superplasticity at cryogenic temperature due to (110) to (100) cross-section reorientation behavior. Interestingly, HEA nanowires can perform exceptional strength-ductility trade-offs at cryogenic temperatures. 3.1. Deformation Behavior of Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs

Figure 2 shows the stress–strain curves of the Ag NWs and CoNiCrFeMn HEA NWs at 77, 300, and 1000 K respectively. At 77 K, Ag NW deforms via nucleation and propagation of a partial dislocation from the free surface, leaving a stacking fault inside the NW (see Figure 3 a). As deformation continues, the stacking fault further separates into two twin boundaries, which extend and continue to grow through entire NW. The cross-section area of the NW eventually converts from (110) to (100), resulting in two peaks in the SS curve, as shown in Figure 2 a. The area between two twin boundaries is transformed as also shown in Figure 3 a between 8% to 32% elongation in the Ag NW. The phase transformation is mainly driven by the surface stresses which enable the reduction in surface energy in the nanowire. On further loading, the difference between two boundaries decreases and finally vanishes at around 50% elongation, resulting in an improved work hardening.
